To form the passive with essere in all tenses: è stato scoperto, sarà pubblicato.
To use venire + participle in the simple tenses: viene letto, verrà pubblicato.
To express necessity with andare + participle: va spostato, vanno corretti.
To use si passivante with correct agreement: si vende un giornale, si vendono giornali.
To introduce the agent with "da": scoperto da Giulia, scritto dal giornalista.
To understand the language of a newspaper article and write a letter to the editor.
Florence, March. Historian Rosalia Lo Bianco's discovery has reached the press. Sandro Mancini, a journalist at the "Gazzetta dell'Oltrarno", comes to the workshop to interview Giulia and Matei.
Ms Esposito, how was the child discovered?
It was discovered by chance, during an X-ray. The painting was being analysed before the restoration, as is always done.
Giulia saw it. I was looking at the screen too, but at the wrong part.
Will the child's face be cleaned? Will it be shown to the public?
No. The face must not be uncovered. It was covered by Caravaggio himself, and his choice must be respected.
But can the X-ray be seen?
Yes, it was printed on a panel next to the painting. You can see it very well.
And the archive documents, the ones from 1608?
Those were found by Professor Lo Bianco. The credit must go to her, not to us.
One last question: after the restoration, will the painting stay in Syracuse?
Of course. That painting was painted for Syracuse, and that is where it must stay.
Perfect. The article will be published on Thursday. It's spelled "Popa", with an a at the end, right?
Popa. With an a. Please don't forget.

1. The passive with essere: all tenses
The passive is formed with essere in the required tense + the participle, which agrees with the subject:
The article is read by everyone.
The news had been picked up.
As in English: "was discovered" = è stato scoperto. The participle agrees: la radiografia è stata stampata, i documenti sono stati trovati.
Instead of essere you can use venire, but ONLY in the simple tenses (present, imperfetto, future, conditional, passato remoto). It stresses the action, the process:
In compound tenses venire is NOT used: the correct form is "è stato scoperto", never "è venuto scoperto".
"Il negozio è chiuso" can describe a state (it is closed). "Il negozio viene chiuso alle otto" clearly means the action (it gets closed at eight). Venire removes the ambiguity.
Andare + participle expresses necessity, obligation, a rule:
This letter should have been written earlier.
Va spostato = deve essere spostato. It is very common in instructions: "Il vino va servito fresco", "Il modulo va firmato".
With certain verbs (perdere, smarrire), andare + participle does NOT mean obligation but loss: "Il documento è andato perso" = the document got lost.
With "si" + the verb in the third person you get a passive without an agent. The verb agrees with the noun:
Just like Romanian "se vinde o casă / se vând case" (a house is sold / houses are sold). In compound tenses the auxiliary is essere and the participle agrees: si sono raccolte diecimila firme.
I documenti sono stati trovati da Rosalia.
Un collega ha aggiunto il paragrafo.
Il paragrafo è stato aggiunto da un collega.
Il volto è stato coperto da Caravaggio.
"Da" merges with the article: dal giornalista, dalla professoressa, dagli studenti. In the press you will also see "da parte di": un errore da parte della redazione.
The documents were found by Professor Lo Bianco.
The X-ray was printed on a panel.
The painting was being analysed before the restoration.
The letter will be published on Sunday.
Per quale giornale lavora Sandro Mancini?

Chi ha visto il bambino per primo?
Perché il volto non va scoperto?

The news was first broken on a Tuesday in March, at seven in the morning, by a radio station in Catania. By eight it had already been picked up by three websites. By nine the workshop phone was ringing non-stop. Chiara answered with one hand and held a brush with the other, until Giulia told her to put it down: the restoration, that day, could wait. The world wanted to know who Totò was.

Rosalia Lo Bianco's scholarly article had been published the week before in an art history journal, one of those read by two hundred people around the world. It was thirty pages full of footnotes, dates and Latin quotations. But a journalist in Catania had read it to the end and realised there was a story inside: a poor boy, the son of a washerwoman, hidden for four hundred years under Caravaggio's black and found again by two restorers from Florence.

Around eleven a call came from a Florence newspaper, the Gazzetta dell'Oltrarno. A journalist, Sandro Mancini, was asking for an interview the next day. Giulia hesitated: she didn't like talking about herself. But Bellini, who had dropped by the workshop that morning "just for a coffee", told her: "Say yes. If the story isn't told by you, it will be told by someone else. And badly."

The interview lasted two hours. Mancini was a kind man with a grey beard and a voice recorder as old as the ones from the nineties. He asked a thousand questions, photographed the X-ray and wanted to see Ernesto's small brush. Davide, who had dropped in after school that afternoon, showed him the drawing of Totò he had made for Turi's sign. Mancini photographed it at once. "This has to be published," he said. "Absolutely."

The article came out on Thursday, on the front page, with a huge headline: "Caravaggio's secret child discovered by two Florentine restorers". Graziella bought ten copies at the newsstand in Piazza Santo Spirito. The newsagent, who had known her for forty years, gave her an eleventh one for free. "For the little girl," he said, pointing at Viola in her pushchair. "So when she grows up she'll know her mum was in the paper."

But on the second page the problems began. According to the article, the child had been discovered "by the famous Professor Ernesto Bellini", who, however, had been dead for many years. Matei had become "Matteo Popov, a restorer of Russian origin". And the last paragraph said that the painting, after the restoration, "will be transferred to Rome, where it will be displayed in a national museum". Bellini read the article twice, then said only: "My grandfather would be pleased. He never got this much publicity while he was alive."

Matei, on the other hand, wasn't laughing. "Popov?" he kept repeating, pacing around the workshop. "Popov? My mother will kill me." Chiara tried to console him: "Think about it, I wasn't even named. I was turned into 'an assistant'." Davide, on the contrary, was overjoyed: his drawing had been printed in colour, with the caption "The Totò of Santa Lucia, drawn by David, aged 12". His name was Davide, not David. But he decided that "David" sounded more American, so it was fine as it was.

The real problem, though, came at four in the afternoon, with a phone call from Syracuse. It was Turi, the sacristan, and he was shouting so loudly that Giulia had to hold the phone away from her ear. "They're taking him to Rome? Our Totò? Fifty people have come to the church to protest! The ladies of the neighbourhood want to chain themselves to the altar!" It took Giulia half an hour to calm him down. "Turi, nobody is taking anything away. The painting must not be moved and will not be moved. It's the newspaper's mistake."

But a mistake published on the front page can't be erased with a phone call. By the afternoon the news of the "transfer to Rome" had already been picked up by other newspapers, and in the evening it was even on the regional TV news. A local politician had declared that "Sicily is not to be touched". Another had proposed a petition. On the internet a page called "Totò stays home" had been created, and within a few hours it had been followed by ten thousand people.

That evening a family council was held in the kitchen. Graziella was cooking, Marco was slicing the bread, and Lupino, even though it wasn't Sunday, had been let in secretly and was waiting under the table for something to fall. "We have to ask for a correction," said Marco. "The paper has to publish the correction." "A correction is read by a tenth of the people who read the article," replied Bellini, who had stayed for dinner. "I know from experience. Once a newspaper wrote that I had lost a painting. The correction was printed on page thirty-two, under the mattress advert."

It was then that Pietro raised his hand, as if at school. "What if we write a letter to the editor? Letters are read by everyone. Grandma only reads those." Graziella confirmed it without turning round from the stove: "It's true. The news makes me sad. Letters, on the other hand, make me laugh." Bellini looked at Pietro with respect. "The boy is right," he said. "And the letter must be written by him."

Pietro worked on it until midnight, with the help of Matei, of Davide (on the phone) and of a dictionary. Giulia checked the facts, Bellini checked the commas. The letter was short and began like this: "Dear Editor, my name is Pietro, I am eleven years old and in your article on Thursday I found three mistakes. I am pointing them out because my teacher says that mistakes must not be hidden: they must be corrected."

Then came the mistakes, one by one. "One: the child was not discovered by Ernesto Bellini, who died many years ago, but by Giulia and Matei, who live above my grandmother's trattoria. Two: Matei's name is not Popov but Popa, and he isn't Russian but Romanian, from Sibiu. His mother knits the most beautiful jumpers in the world and she is offended. Three, and most important: the painting is not going to Rome. In four hundred years it has never moved, and it won't move now."

The letter ended with a postscript, added at the last minute by Pietro without asking anyone's permission: "P.S. The drawing of Totò was not made by 'David' but by Davide, who is my best friend and draws better than anyone. But he likes 'David', so you can leave that mistake." Reading it, Bellini laughed until he cried. "This postscript," he said, "must be left exactly as it is. Don't touch a single comma."

The letter was sent by email the next morning at eight. At ten Sandro Mancini phoned the workshop. He was terribly embarrassed. He explained that the article had been written by him, but that the last paragraph had been added in the newsroom by a colleague, who had mixed up the Totò of Syracuse with another painting that really was going to Rome. "I'm terribly sorry," he said. "And the boy's letter… the editor read it aloud at the meeting. It will be published on Sunday. On the front page."

On Sunday morning Graziella went to the newsstand at half past six, before it had even opened. The newsagent was cutting the string on the bundles of newspapers. He opened one, looked at the front page and whistled. At the top, next to the main headline, there was a box with Pietro's photo and the words: "Three mistakes and a postscript: an eleven-year-old's lesson in journalism". Below, the letter had been printed in full, with Davide's drawing. This time in colour and with the right name.

The rest happened quickly. The letter was read in class by Pietro's teacher, then it was picked up by a Catania newspaper and finally by a national radio station. In Syracuse, Turi printed it and hung it next to the painting, under the new sign, with four drawing pins. The page "Totò stays home" changed its name: now it was called "Totò never left", and its ten thousand followers, instead of politics, started discussing Caravaggio, washerwomen and seventeenth-century bread.

On Monday an envelope arrived at the workshop addressed to "Matei Popa (not Popov)". Inside was a handwritten note from Sandro Mancini: "To apologise, I invite you all to visit the newsroom. The boy may bring his artist friend. Coffee, croissants and a lesson on how a newspaper is made will be provided. Mistakes included." Pietro and Davide spent the week preparing their questions. Davide above all wanted to know one thing: whether drawings got paid for at the newspaper.

That evening Doina phoned from Sibiu. Someone had sent her a photo of the article with the mistake, and she, in protest, had already started a jumper with POPA written on it in huge letters. "That way," she told Matei, "next time they photograph you, your name is already written." Matei promised he would wear it. Giulia promised she would photograph it. And Bellini, in his black notebook, wrote under the date: "Today I learned something. A newspaper got it wrong three times. A child corrected it only once. And that was enough."
